The Complete PPC Guide for Home Service Businesses

Complete PPC guide for home service businesses. Includes keyword strategy, ad copy, landing pages, budget recommendations, and cost per lead benchmarks.

OnwardCraft Team Growth Strategists

If you run a home service business and your phone is not ringing consistently from paid search, you are leaving revenue on the table every single day. This guide covers everything you need to know about PPC for contractors: how Google Ads actually works, what keywords to bid on, how to write ads that convert, what landing pages produce 6-12% conversion rates, how much to spend, and how to track every dollar back to booked jobs. Whether you are spending $1,500 a month or $15,000, the frameworks in this article will help you lower your cost per lead and increase your return on ad spend.

What Is PPC for Contractors and Why Does It Matter in 2026?

PPC for contractors is paid advertising where you pay only when a potential customer clicks your ad. For home service businesses, this almost always means Google Ads: the sponsored listings that appear at the top of search results when someone types "emergency plumber near me" or "HVAC repair [city name]." Unlike SEO, which can take 6-12 months to generate consistent leads, PPC delivers qualified prospects within 24-48 hours of launch.

The U.S. home services market reached $842 billion in 2026, according to Mordor Intelligence. Yet only 55% of home service companies have adopted any digital marketing strategy, and over 50% still operate without a dedicated website. This gap between consumer behavior and contractor readiness is exactly why paid search for contractors remains one of the highest-ROI marketing channels available. When 84% of bookings start on a mobile device and 70% of homeowners prefer to book services online, showing up at the exact moment someone searches for your service is not optional. It is survival.

How Google Ads Works for Home Service Businesses

Google Ads operates on a real-time auction system. Every time someone searches a keyword you are bidding on, Google runs an auction in milliseconds. Your Ad Rank determines whether your ad shows and in what position. Ad Rank is calculated as: Max CPC Bid x Quality Score x Expected Impact of Ad Assets. This means a contractor with a Quality Score of 8 can outrank a competitor bidding twice as much with a Quality Score of 4. Quality Score is not a vanity metric. It directly controls how much you pay per click.

Here is what that looks like in practice. A plumbing contractor in Denver bidding on "emergency plumber Denver" with a $20 max CPC and a Quality Score of 8 will pay approximately $12.60 per click. A competitor bidding $25 with a Quality Score of 4 will pay roughly $18.75 per click and still appear below the better-optimized ad. Over 1,000 clicks, that is a $6,150 difference in cost for the same traffic. This is why contractor PPC is not about who has the biggest budget. It is about who understands the system.

The Two Primary PPC Channels for Contractors

Contractors have two main paid search options: Google Search Ads and Google Local Services Ads (LSAs). Search Ads are the traditional pay-per-click model. You write ads, choose keywords, set bids, and pay when someone clicks. LSAs are a pay-per-lead model where Google verifies your license and insurance, displays a Google Verified badge, and charges you only when a customer calls or messages through the ad. LSAs appear above Search Ads, making them the most visible real estate on the page.

Data from 2026 shows that contractors running both channels together generate 23% more total lead volume than either channel alone. The recommended budget split for most contractors is approximately 60% LSA and 40% Search Ads initially, then optimizing toward cost per booked job rather than cost per lead. LSAs average $25-$120 per lead depending on trade, while Search Ads average $90.92 per lead across all home services.

Why Most Contractor PPC Accounts Underperform

Industry audits consistently show that most contractor PPC accounts waste 30-50% of their budget before generating the first qualified call. The reasons are predictable: broad match keywords without negative keyword protection, generic ad copy that does not match search intent, traffic sent to homepages instead of dedicated landing pages, and no call tracking to measure what actually converts. These are not advanced problems. They are foundational errors that compound over time.

The contractors who win at PPC treat it as a system, not a switch. They build negative keyword lists before launching. They create service-specific landing pages with message match. They track calls, forms, and booked jobs in a CRM. They review search term reports weekly. They test ad copy monthly. This guide will show you exactly how to build that system.

PPC Fundamentals: How the Auction, Quality Score, and Ad Rank Actually Work

To run profitable PPC for contractors, you need to understand the mechanics of the Google Ads auction. Most contractors treat PPC like a vending machine: put money in, get leads out. The reality is more like a stock market where your competitors, your Quality Score, and your ad relevance all determine whether you win the auction and at what price.

The Real-Time Auction Explained

Every Google search triggers an auction. Google evaluates every advertiser bidding on that keyword and assigns an Ad Rank. The formula is: Ad Rank = Max CPC Bid x Quality Score x Expected Impact of Ad Assets. The advertiser with the highest Ad Rank gets position one. The advertiser with the second-highest gets position two. Your actual cost per click is calculated as: (Ad Rank of the advertiser below you / Your Quality Score) + $0.01. This means improving your Quality Score lowers your CPC even if your bid stays the same.

Let us walk through a concrete example. Three HVAC contractors bid on "AC repair Phoenix."

  • Contractor A: $18 max CPC, Quality Score 9, Ad Rank = 162
  • Contractor B: $25 max CPC, Quality Score 5, Ad Rank = 125
  • Contractor C: $15 max CPC, Quality Score 7, Ad Rank = 105

Contractor A wins position one despite bidding less than Contractor B. Contractor A's actual CPC is (125 / 9) + $0.01 = $13.90. Contractor B pays (105 / 5) + $0.01 = $21.01 for position two. Contractor A gets better placement at 34% lower cost because they invested in Quality Score. This is the single most important concept in contractor PPC.

Quality Score: The Three Components That Control Your Costs

Quality Score is a 1-10 diagnostic score assigned to each keyword. It consists of three components: Expected Click-Through Rate, Ad Relevance, and Landing Page Experience. Each is rated Below Average, Average, or Above Average. Your overall Quality Score is the weighted average, with Expected CTR carrying the most influence.

Expected CTR measures how likely your ad is to be clicked compared to other ads showing for the same keyword. Google looks at your historical performance. If your ad consistently gets clicked at a higher rate than competitors, Google rewards you with lower costs and better positions. For home service PPC, this means writing headlines that directly match the search query. If someone searches "emergency water heater repair," your headline should say exactly that, not "Full-Service Plumbing Company."

Ad Relevance measures how closely your ad copy matches the keyword and search intent. Google checks whether your keywords appear in your headlines and descriptions. For contractors, the most common mistake is using the same generic ad across all services. A roofing ad should talk about roofs. A plumbing ad should talk about pipes. This sounds obvious, but we audit accounts every week where one ad group serves 47 unrelated keywords with identical copy.

Landing Page Experience measures how useful and relevant your page is to someone who clicks your ad. In 2026, page load speed accounts for 35% of this score, up from 20% in 2025. Google measures Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint under 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint under 200 milliseconds, and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. Accounts with Below Average landing page experience pay 47% higher CPC and suffer 23% lower ad visibility.

How Quality Score Translates to Real Dollar Savings

The financial impact of Quality Score is non-linear and dramatic. Moving from a Quality Score of 5 to 8 reduces your CPC by approximately 30%. Moving from 5 to 10 can reduce it by 50% or more. Conversely, dropping from 5 to 3 increases your CPC by 67%. Here is the full mapping:

For a contractor spending $5,000 per month on Google Ads, improving average Quality Score from 5 to 8 means getting the same traffic for $3,150. That $1,850 monthly savings equals $22,200 per year. Or, reinvested at the same budget, it means 59% more clicks and leads for the same spend. Every point of Quality Score improvement reduces CPC by approximately 8-10%.

Ad Assets and Extensions: Free Real Estate You Are Probably Underusing

Ad assets, formerly called extensions, are additional pieces of information Google can append to your ads at no extra cost. They directly improve your Ad Rank and click-through rate. For contractors, the most impactful extensions are:

  • Call extensions: Display your phone number and enable click-to-call on mobile. Essential for emergency services.
  • Location extensions: Show your business address and link to Google Maps. Builds local trust.
  • Sitelink extensions: Link to specific pages like "Financing Options," "Service Areas," "Customer Reviews," and "Request a Quote."
  • Callout extensions: Highlight key selling points like "Licensed & Insured," "24/7 Emergency Service," "Free Estimates," and "10-Year Warranty."
  • Structured snippets: List your services: "Services: Roofing, Siding, Gutters, Windows."
  • Price extensions: Show starting prices for common services. Pre-qualifies clicks and improves lead quality.

Contractors who use all relevant extensions typically see a 15-20% improvement in CTR. Google rewards this with better Ad Rank and lower CPC. The setup takes 30 minutes. The benefit compounds for years.

Account Structure: The Foundation of Every Profitable Campaign

Your account structure determines how well you can control bids, write relevant ads, and optimize performance. The recommended structure for contractor PPC is one campaign per service line, with tightly themed ad groups underneath. Here is how an HVAC contractor should structure their account:

  • Campaign 1: AC Repair & Emergency (highest intent, highest bids)
  • Campaign 2: AC Installation & Replacement (planned purchase, medium bids)
  • Campaign 3: Heating Repair & Furnace (seasonal, variable bids)
  • Campaign 4: HVAC Maintenance & Tune-Ups (lower intent, lower bids)
  • Campaign 5: Indoor Air Quality (niche service, test budget)

Each campaign gets its own budget, its own landing page, and its own bidding strategy. This prevents high-intent emergency keywords from being starved of budget by lower-intent maintenance keywords. It also lets you write ads that speak directly to the specific need: "AC Broke? Same-Day Repair in [City]" for emergency repair versus "Replace Your Old AC. 0% Financing Available" for installation.

The Difference Between Search, Display, and Performance Max

Search campaigns show text ads on Google search results pages. They capture active intent: someone is searching for what you offer right now. This is where 80% of contractor PPC budgets should go.

Display campaigns show image ads on websites, apps, and YouTube. They are for remarketing: showing ads to people who visited your site but did not convert. Display is not for cold prospecting in home services. It is for staying top-of-mind during a 2-4 week decision cycle.

Performance Max (PMax) is Google's automated campaign type that runs across Search, Display, YouTube, Gmail, Maps, and Discover. In 2026, PMax accounts for 45% of all Google Ads conversions. For contractors with 50+ monthly conversions, PMax can supplement Search campaigns. For smaller accounts, it often wastes budget on low-quality placements. Start with Search. Add PMax only after you have conversion data and a solid negative keyword foundation.

Keyword Strategy: How to Find, Group, and Bid on the Keywords That Actually Book Jobs

Keyword strategy is where most contractor PPC accounts succeed or fail. You can have perfect ad copy, beautiful landing pages, and flawless tracking, but if you are bidding on the wrong keywords, none of it matters. The goal is not to get the most clicks. The goal is to get clicks from people who are ready to hire a contractor right now.

The Three Tiers of Contractor Keywords

Not all keywords are equal. They fall into three tiers based on buyer intent. Your bidding strategy should treat them differently.

Tier 1: Hire-Ready Keywords These are searches from people who have decided to hire a contractor and are looking for the right one. They convert at 8-15%. Examples include "hire kitchen remodeling contractor," "emergency plumber near me," "licensed electrician [city]," and "HVAC company [zip code]." These keywords deserve your highest bids and most dedicated landing pages.

Tier 2: Evaluating Keywords These searches come from people who are comparing options or gathering information before making a decision. They convert at 3-7%. Examples include "kitchen remodeling cost," "best HVAC company [city]," "roof repair estimate," and "how much does furnace replacement cost." Bid medium on these. Use them to build your pipeline, but do not let them consume your entire budget.

Tier 3: Research Keywords These are informational searches from people who are not ready to hire anyone. They convert at 0.5-2%. Examples include "kitchen remodeling ideas," "how long does an HVAC system last," and "types of roofing materials." For most contractors, these should be excluded from PPC or bid at very low levels. They are better suited for SEO content marketing.

Tier 2Evaluating"[service] cost," "best [trade] [city]," "[service] estimate"3-7%Medium

Commercial Intent Modifiers to Target

Certain words signal commercial intent. When they appear in a search query, the person is much more likely to become a paying customer. Prioritize keywords containing these modifiers:

  • Hire signals: hire, contractor, company, professional, expert
  • Location signals: near me, [city name], [zip code], [neighborhood], local
  • Action signals: book, schedule, call, get a quote, estimate
  • Urgency signals: emergency, same day, 24/7, now, ASAP
  • Qualification signals: licensed, insured, certified, bonded, BBB

A keyword like "emergency plumber near me" contains three commercial modifiers: emergency, near me, and the implicit hiring intent of searching for a service provider. A keyword like "how to fix a leaky faucet" contains zero commercial modifiers and should be excluded from your PPC campaigns.

Keyword Match Types: Exact, Phrase, and Broad

Google Ads offers three match types that control how loosely your keywords match to actual search queries. Your match type strategy determines how much control you have over your traffic quality.

Exact Match [keyword] triggers only for the exact keyword or very close variants with the same intent. Example: [emergency plumber near me] matches "emergency plumbers near me" but not "plumber jobs near me." Exact match gives you maximum relevance, highest conversion rates, and least wasted spend. It also has the lowest volume and typically the highest CPC. Use exact match for your Tier 1 hire-ready keywords.

Phrase Match "keyword" triggers when the query contains your keyword phrase in order, with words before or after. Example: "water heater repair" matches "best water heater repair service" and "water heater repair near me." Phrase match offers a good balance of reach and control. It is the workhorse match type for most contractor campaigns.

Broad Match keyword triggers for anything Google considers "related." Example: plumber matches "plumber salary," "plumber training," "plumber movie," and "how to become a plumber." Broad match is dangerous for contractors. Without aggressive negative keywords, it can burn 25-40% of your budget on irrelevant clicks. Use broad match only for keyword discovery with heavy negative protection, or when you have 50+ monthly conversions and Smart Bidding can filter out the noise.

2026 Recommendation: Start with phrase match and exact match. Use broad match only with aggressive negative keywords and only after you have established conversion tracking and a baseline of performance data.

The Negative Keyword Architecture Every Contractor Needs

Negative keywords prevent your ads from showing for irrelevant searches. They are the single most powerful tool for reducing wasted spend. Most contractor accounts we audit have fewer than 50 negative keywords. A properly built account has 300 or more. Here is the three-layer architecture we use for every client.

Layer 1: Universal Negatives (Apply to All Contractors) These exclude searches that no contractor wants to pay for. They fall into categories:

  • Job seekers: jobs, hiring, salary, career, apprentice, training, certification, license requirements, school
  • DIY researchers: DIY, how to, tutorial, fix it yourself, step by step, do it yourself
  • Non-buyers: free, cheap, discount, pro bono, coupon, bargain
  • Product shoppers: buy, purchase, parts, supplies, for sale, Home Depot, Lowes, Amazon
  • Review/complaint: reviews, complaints, lawsuit, scam, rip off, BBB (when not your own)
  • Information seekers: cost, price, how much, average, estimate, quotes (use selectively for PPC)

Layer 2: Search Campaign-Specific Exclusions These are more aggressive negatives for traditional Search campaigns:

  • Comparison shoppers: vs, versus, compared to, alternative, best, top rated
  • Wrong segment: commercial, business, office, industrial, warehouse (if you are residential-only)
  • Service boundaries: maintenance, inspection, preventive (if you are emergency-only)
  • Project size: new construction, installation, build (if you are repair-only)
  • Future intent: someday, eventually, planning, future, next year

Layer 3: Trade-Specific Negatives Each trade has its own set of commonly missed negatives:

Building Your Keyword List: A Step-by-Step Process

Here is the exact process we use to build keyword lists for contractor clients:

  1. Start with seed keywords. List every service you offer. For an HVAC company: AC repair, AC installation, furnace repair, furnace replacement, heat pump installation, duct cleaning, thermostat installation.
  2. Expand with location modifiers. Combine each service with every city, zip code, and neighborhood you serve. AC repair Phoenix, AC repair 85018, AC repair Arcadia.
  3. Add intent modifiers. Append commercial intent words: emergency AC repair Phoenix, same day AC repair Phoenix, licensed AC repair Phoenix.
  4. Use Google Keyword Planner. Enter your seed keywords to find search volume, competition, and suggested bid ranges. Look for keywords with commercial intent and reasonable volume.
  5. Check competitor ads. Search your target keywords and note what competitors are bidding on. Use tools like SEMrush or SpyFu to see their full keyword lists.
  6. Organize into ad groups. Group keywords by theme. Each ad group should have 3-10 closely related keywords. Never put "emergency plumber" and "bathroom remodel" in the same ad group.
  7. Build negative keywords before launch. Apply all three layers of negatives before you spend your first dollar.

Bid Strategy by Match Type and Intent

Your bids should reflect the value of each keyword. Here is the framework:

Match TypeRelative BidRationale
Exact match (Tier 1)HighestMaximum relevance, highest conversion rate
Phrase match (Tier 1)HighStrong intent with slightly broader reach
Exact match (Tier 2)MediumEvaluating intent, longer sales cycle
Phrase match (Tier 2)Medium-lowBroader reach, lower immediate conversion
Broad match (any tier)LowestHighest risk, use only with heavy negatives

Weekly Keyword Optimization Habits

The search terms report shows you exactly what people typed before clicking your ad. Review it every week. Every irrelevant query becomes a new negative keyword. Your target: less than 5% of matched search terms should be irrelevant after your first two weeks. If you are seeing more than 15% irrelevant traffic, your negative keyword list has major gaps.

Also look for high-performing search terms that are not in your keyword list. Add them as exact match keywords with their own dedicated ad group and landing page. This is how you scale what works.

Ad Copy for Contractors: How to Write Google Ads That Get Clicked and Convert

Your ad copy is the only thing standing between a searcher and your competitor. You have three headlines of 30 characters each, two descriptions of 90 characters each, and a handful of extensions to convince someone to click your ad instead of the three or four others on the page. In 2026, Google uses Responsive Search Ads (RSAs) exclusively. You write up to 15 headlines and 4 descriptions, and Google's AI tests combinations to find what performs best.

The Psychology of High-Converting Contractor Ads

Homeowners searching for contractors are in a state of mild anxiety. Their AC is broken. Their roof is leaking. Their electrical panel is sparking. They need help fast, but they are also worried about getting ripped off, hiring someone unqualified, or paying too much. Your ad copy must simultaneously address their urgency and their fear.

The most effective contractor ads use a combination of five psychological triggers:

  • Urgency: "Same-Day Service," "24/7 Emergency Repair," "Book Before [Season]"
  • Social proof: "Rated 4.9 Stars by 500+ Homeowners," "Voted Best [Trade] 2024"
  • Risk reversal: "Free Estimate," "No Obligation," "100% Satisfaction Guaranteed"
  • Authority: "Licensed & Insured," "25+ Years Experience," "BBB A+ Rated"
  • Specificity: "Repairs from $299," "2-Hour Response Time," "Serving [City] Since 2005"

Data from 2026 shows that ads using urgency language see a 22% higher CTR. Ads with specific pricing see 20% fewer irrelevant clicks, which improves lead quality and reduces wasted spend. Ads with social proof generate higher-quality leads who are pre-sold on your reputation.

Responsive Search Ad Structure for Contractors

Google recommends writing at least 10 headlines and 3-4 descriptions per RSA. We recommend 12-14 headlines and 4 descriptions. Here is the formula:

Headline Categories (write 2-3 of each):

  • Service + Location: "Emergency Plumber in [City]," "AC Repair [Neighborhood]"
  • Urgency: "Same-Day Service Available," "24/7 Emergency Repairs"
  • Offer: "Free Estimate," "Free Inspection," "0% Financing"
  • Social Proof: "500+ 5-Star Reviews," "Rated #1 in [City]"
  • Trust: "Licensed & Insured," "BBB A+ Rated," "Family-Owned Since [Year]"
  • Differentiator: "Upfront Pricing," "No Hidden Fees," "Lifetime Warranty"

Description Categories (write 1-2 of each):

  • Problem + Solution: "Leaky roof? Our certified technicians diagnose and repair all roofing issues. Free inspection included."
  • Process: "Call us for a free estimate. We show up on time, explain your options, and never pressure you to buy."
  • Guarantee: "100% satisfaction guaranteed. Licensed, insured, and background-checked technicians. Serving [City] for 20+ years."
  • Offer Details: "0% financing for 12 months. Military and senior discounts available. Schedule your free consultation today."

Pinning Strategy: When and How to Control Headline Placement

By default, Google tests all headline combinations. You can pin specific headlines to specific positions. Use pinning strategically:

  • Pin Position 1: Your most important message, usually service + location or urgency. Example: "Emergency AC Repair [City]"
  • Pin Position 2: Your offer or differentiator. Example: "Same-Day Service Available"
  • Pin Position 3: Social proof or trust signal. Example: "500+ 5-Star Reviews"

Do not pin every headline. Google needs flexibility to test combinations. Pin only your 2-3 most critical messages. If you pin more than 5 headlines, you severely limit Google's ability to optimize.

Ad Extensions Every Contractor Should Use

Extensions are free additional information that Google appends to your ads. They improve CTR, Ad Rank, and lead quality. Here are the must-haves:

Sitelink Extensions: Link to high-value pages. Examples: "Financing Options," "Service Areas," "Customer Reviews," "Request a Quote," "Emergency Services," "Our Process." Each sitelink should have its own descriptive text (2 lines of 25 characters).

Callout Extensions: Short value propositions. Examples: "Licensed & Insured," "24/7 Emergency Service," "Free Quotes," "10-Year Warranty," "Same-Day Service," "Military Discounts."

Structured Snippets: Lists of services or features. Header: Services. Values: Roofing, Siding, Gutters, Windows, Doors. Or Header: Brands. Values: Carrier, Trane, Lennox, Goodman.

Call Extensions: Essential for mobile. Display your phone number and enable click-to-call. Set business hours so the extension only shows when you can answer.

Location Extensions: Show your address and link to Google Maps. Critical for local trust.

Price Extensions: Set expectations upfront. Examples: "HVAC Tune-Up from $89," "Drain Cleaning from $149," "Roof Inspection Free." Price extensions filter out price shoppers and improve lead quality.

Ad Copy Refresh Cadence

Creative fatigue is real. After 6-8 weeks, CTR typically drops 15-20% as the same audience sees the same ads repeatedly. Schedule ad copy refreshes every 6-8 weeks. Rotate in new angles, update seasonal messaging, and test new offers. Keep your top-performing headlines and replace the bottom 30%.

Landing Pages for PPC: The Difference Between a 2% and a 12% Conversion Rate

Your landing page is where clicks turn into leads. You can have the best keywords and the most compelling ads, but if your landing page is slow, confusing, or untrustworthy, you are burning money. Industry data shows that service-specific landing pages convert at 6-12%, while generic homepages convert at 1-3%. For a contractor spending $5,000 per month, that is the difference between 30 leads and 120 leads.

Message Match: The Non-Negotiable Rule

Message match means your landing page headline must match the promise made in your ad. If your ad says "Same-Day AC Repair in Phoenix," your landing page must lead with "Same-Day AC Repair in Phoenix." Not "Welcome to ABC Heating & Cooling." Not "Your Trusted HVAC Partner Since 1998." The exact service, the exact location, the exact promise.

When message match is broken, visitors experience cognitive dissonance. They clicked expecting one thing and landed on something else. Bounce rates spike. Conversion rates plummet. Google's Quality Score drops. Your CPC rises. Message match is not a best practice. It is a requirement.

Use Dynamic Keyword Insertion (DKI) to personalize headlines based on the search query. A single landing page can display "Emergency Plumber in Arcadia" or "Emergency Plumber in Scottsdale" depending on where the visitor came from. This level of personalization can increase conversion rates by 15-25%.

The Anatomy of a High-Converting Contractor Landing Page

Every contractor PPC landing page needs these elements, in this approximate order:

1. Headline (Above the Fold) Match the ad exactly. Use the same words the visitor searched. Keep it under 10 words. Example: "Same-Day AC Repair in Phoenix. Free Estimate."

2. Subheadline Expand on the headline with a benefit or differentiator. Example: "Licensed technicians arrive in 2 hours or less. Upfront pricing. No hidden fees."

3. Primary CTA One clear action above the fold. For mobile: a prominent click-to-call button. For desktop: a short form. Example: "Call (555) 123-4567" or "Get Your Free Estimate."

4. Trust Signals (Near the CTA) Place these within the first 100 pixels of the page: "Licensed & Insured," "BBB A+ Rated," "500+ 5-Star Reviews," "20+ Years in Business." Trust signals near the CTA increase form submissions by 20-30%.

5. Short Benefit List 3-5 bullet points explaining why someone should choose you. Example: "Same-day service guaranteed," "Upfront pricing before any work begins," "Licensed, bonded, and insured," "100% satisfaction guarantee," "Financing available."

6. Social Proof Real customer reviews with names and locations. "ABC Fixed our AC same day. Professional, friendly, and fair pricing. - Sarah M., Phoenix." Include star ratings and total review count.

7. Service Explanation Briefly explain what happens when they contact you. Step 1: Call or fill out the form. Step 2: We diagnose the issue. Step 3: You get upfront pricing. Step 4: We complete the repair. This reduces anxiety about the unknown.

8. Secondary CTA Repeat your primary call-to-action at the bottom of the page. Do not make visitors scroll back up.

Mobile-First Design for Home Service PPC

Over 62% of home service searches happen on mobile devices. Your landing page must be designed for thumbs, not mice. Key requirements:

  • Click-to-call button: Prominent, sticky, and above the fold. Use tel: links so one tap initiates a call.
  • Thumb-friendly tap targets: Buttons and form fields must be at least 44x44 pixels.
  • 16px+ font size: Google penalizes pages with small text that requires pinching to zoom.
  • Fast load time: Under 2 seconds on 4G. Every additional second reduces conversions by 7%.
  • No pop-ups on mobile: Google penalizes intrusive interstitials. Use inline forms instead.

Form Optimization: Short Forms Win

Every field you add to a form reduces completion rates. For contractor PPC, ask for the minimum information needed to follow up:

  • Name
  • Phone number
  • Service needed (dropdown)
  • Zip code or address

That is it. Four fields. Do not ask for email unless you have an email nurture sequence. Do not ask for "best time to call" unless your scheduling system requires it. Do not ask for budget range. You can gather that information during the follow-up call.

Multi-step forms can improve completion rates by 30-50%. Step 1 asks for zip code and service type. Step 2 asks for name and phone. Step 3 confirms the details. The psychological principle is commitment and consistency: once someone starts, they are more likely to finish.

Speed and Technical Performance

In 2026, landing page speed is not just a user experience issue. It is a Quality Score component and a direct ranking factor. Here are the targets:

MetricTargetTool to Measure
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)Under 2.5 secondsGoogle PageSpeed Insights
Interaction to Next Paint (INP)Under 200 millisecondsGoogle PageSpeed Insights
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)Under 0.1Google PageSpeed Insights
Total page sizeUnder 1.5 MBGTmetrix
Server response timeUnder 200 millisecondsWebPageTest

Practical speed improvements: compress images to WebP or AVIF format, use a content delivery network (CDN), minify CSS and JavaScript, lazy-load images below the fold, and choose a fast hosting provider. A contractor landing page with a 5-second load time that drops to 2 seconds will typically see a 15-20% conversion rate improvement.

Remove Navigation and Distractions

Your PPC landing page should have one goal: convert the visitor into a lead. Remove the main website navigation menu. Remove links to your blog, about page, and portfolio. Remove social media icons. Every exit path you eliminate increases conversion rates. Studies show that removing navigation alone can boost conversions by up to 336%.

Include only these links: your phone number (click-to-call), the form submission, and optionally a link to your reviews or financing page if those are key objections. That is it.

A/B Testing Your Landing Pages

Never settle for your first landing page. Test variations systematically. Here are high-impact tests for contractor PPC:

  • Headline: "Same-Day AC Repair" vs. "AC Repair from $89" vs. "Phoenix's #1 AC Repair Company"
  • CTA button: "Get Free Estimate" vs. "Call Now" vs. "Schedule Service"
  • Form length: 4 fields vs. 3 fields vs. multi-step
  • Trust signals: BBB badge vs. review count vs. years in business
  • Images: Technician photo vs. before/after project photos vs. no image
  • Urgency: "Limited Appointments" banner vs. no banner

Run each test until you have at least 100 conversions per variant. Use Google Optimize, Unbounce, or VWO for testing. Document winners and feed insights into your next test cycle.

Budget and Bidding: How Much to Spend and How to Allocate It

The most common question we hear from contractors is: "How much should I spend on Google Ads?" The honest answer is: it depends on your market, your trade, your goals, and your capacity to handle leads. But there are clear benchmarks and frameworks that remove the guesswork.

Minimum Viable Budgets by Contractor Type

Google's algorithms need data to optimize. If your budget is too small, you will not generate enough clicks or conversions for the system to learn what works. Here are the minimums:

Contractor TypeMonthly Ad SpendExpected LeadsNotes
Starter/Testing$1,500-$3,00010-25Minimum to generate consistent data
Growth-Focused$3,000-$5,00025-50Allows A/B testing and optimization
Established/Multi-location$5,000-$10,000+50-120+Full market coverage, seasonal scaling
Market Dominator$10,000-$20,000+100-250+Multiple trades, multiple markets

These are ad spend numbers, not total marketing budgets. Add management fees if you work with an agency: typically $1,500-$4,000 per month for professional PPC management, or 15-20% of ad spend for larger accounts.

Cost Per Lead Benchmarks by Trade

Based on 2025-2026 data from LocaliQ, WordStream, and agency benchmarks:

Remember: do not optimize for lowest CPL. Optimize for cost per booked job. A $228 roofing lead that closes a $15,000 job is far more valuable than a $47 cleaning lead for a $150 service.

Budget as a Percentage of Revenue

Another way to think about PPC budget is as a percentage of revenue. The Small Business Administration recommends spending 7-8% of gross revenue on marketing. For growth-focused contractors, 10-15% is more realistic. Here is how to allocate:

Annual RevenueTotal Marketing BudgetGoogle Ads (Monthly)Goal
$200K-$500K$15K-$50K/year$1,500-$3,000Consistent lead flow

Bidding Strategy by Campaign Phase

Your bidding strategy should evolve as your account matures:

Launch Phase (Days 1-45): Use Manual CPC or Enhanced CPC with a maximum CPC cap. You need to control costs while Google gathers data. Set daily budgets high enough to get meaningful clicks. A $100/day budget with a $15 CPC gets you 6-7 clicks. That is not enough data. Aim for at least 15-20 clicks per day per campaign.

Growth Phase (Month 2-3): Once you have 30+ conversions per month, switch to Maximize Conversions or Target CPA. Set your Target CPA based on actual cost-per-booked-job data, not wishful thinking. If your average job value is $8,000 and you close 25% of leads, you can afford a $200 CPA. If your average job is $800 and you close 20%, your max CPA is $80.

Scale Phase (Month 4+): With 100+ conversions and revenue tracking in place, use Target ROAS if you can attribute revenue to campaigns. Otherwise, continue with Target CPA and increase budgets only where return is proven. The 70/20/10 rule applies: 70% of budget to proven campaigns, 20% to growth tests, 10% to experiments.

Geographic Bid Adjustments

Not all zip codes convert equally. Use geographic bid adjustments to pay more for high-converting areas and less for low-converting ones. If zip code 85018 generates a 12% conversion rate and zip code 85032 generates 4%, increase bids by 20% in 85018 and decrease by 15% in 85032. Review and adjust these monthly based on conversion data, not click volume.

Seasonal Budget Adjustments

Home services are seasonal. HVAC companies should increase budgets by 40-60% in summer and winter peak seasons. Roofing companies should surge spend before and after storm seasons. Pool companies should front-load budget in spring. Plan your annual budget in quarterly allocations, not equal monthly spends.

Tracking and Measurement: How to Know If Your PPC Is Actually Profitable

Most contractors track the wrong metrics. They look at clicks, impressions, and even cost per lead. But the metric that matters is cost per booked job. If you do not know which keywords, ads, and campaigns generate actual revenue, you are flying blind. This section shows you how to build a tracking system that connects every PPC dollar to real business outcomes.

The Measurement Hierarchy for Contractor PPC

Track metrics at four levels, from least to most important:

  1. Traffic metrics: Impressions, clicks, CTR, CPC. These tell you if your ads are visible and appealing. They do not tell you if you are making money.
  2. Lead metrics: Form submissions, phone calls, cost per lead. These tell you if your landing pages are working. They still do not tell you if you are making money.
  3. Sales metrics: Appointments booked, proposals sent, deals closed, cost per booked job. These tell you if your sales process is converting leads.
  4. Revenue metrics: Revenue per lead, return on ad spend (ROAS), customer lifetime value. These tell you if your PPC is profitable.

Contractors who stop at level 2 optimize for cheaper leads, not more revenue. A $50 lead that never books is more expensive than a $150 lead that closes a $10,000 job.

Call Tracking: The Non-Negotiable Foundation

For home service businesses, 60-70% of PPC conversions happen over the phone. If you are not tracking calls, you are missing most of your data. Call tracking works by displaying unique phone numbers based on the traffic source. A visitor from Google Ads sees one number. A visitor from organic search sees another. When they call, you know exactly which campaign, ad group, and keyword generated the lead.

Essential call tracking features for contractors:

  • Dynamic Number Insertion (DNI): Automatically swaps phone numbers based on traffic source, campaign, or keyword.
  • Call recording: Record calls for quality review, sales coaching, and dispute resolution.
  • Call duration filtering: Set minimum call length for conversion tracking. We recommend 60-90 seconds for most trades. A 10-second wrong-number call should not count as a conversion.
  • Call transcription: AI transcription identifies booking intent, objections, and follow-up needs.
  • CRM integration: Automatically log calls as leads in your CRM with source attribution.

Recommended call tracking tools: CallRail, WhatConverts, and Invoca. CallRail starts at $45/month. WhatConverts starts at $30/month. Either is a fraction of what you will save by eliminating wasted spend.

Form Tracking and Conversion Actions

Set up conversion tracking in Google Ads for every lead generation action:

  • Form submissions: Thank-you page load or form submit event in Google Tag Manager.
  • Phone calls from ads: Click-to-call button clicks on mobile.
  • Phone calls from website: Calls to your tracking numbers from landing pages.
  • Chat initiations: If you use live chat, track chat starts as conversions.
  • Appointment bookings: If you have online scheduling, track completed bookings.

Assign different values to different conversion types if possible. A booked appointment is worth more than a form submission. An emergency call is worth more than a maintenance inquiry.

CRM Integration and Closed-Loop Attribution

The holy grail of PPC measurement is closed-loop attribution: connecting every click to a lead, every lead to a proposal, and every proposal to revenue. This requires integrating your PPC data with your CRM.

Here is how the flow works:

  1. A homeowner clicks your Google Ad for "emergency plumber Phoenix."
  2. They land on your service-specific page and call the tracking number.
  3. CallRail logs the call, records it, and pushes the lead to your CRM (HubSpot, Salesforce, JobNimbus, ServiceTitan).
  4. Your office books an appointment and marks the lead as "Scheduled."
  5. The technician completes the job and marks it as "Closed-Won" with a revenue value of $1,200.
  6. The CRM pushes the revenue data back to Google Ads via offline conversion import.
  7. Google Ads now knows that the keyword "emergency plumber Phoenix" generated $1,200 in revenue.
  8. You increase bids on that keyword and similar ones.

This level of attribution is not theoretical. It is standard practice for contractors spending $3,000+ per month on PPC. The setup takes 2-4 hours. The insights it generates are worth tens of thousands of dollars per year.

Attribution Models: Which One Should You Use?

Google Ads offers several attribution models. Here is how to choose:

ModelHow It WorksBest For
Data-DrivenMachine learning assigns credit based on actual contributionAccounts with 300+ conversions/month
Position-Based (U-Shaped)40% credit to first click, 40% to last click, 20% to middleContractors with mixed brand and non-brand campaigns
Time DecayMore credit to touchpoints closer to conversionEmergency services with short sales cycles
Last Click100% credit to the final touchpointSimple accounts with one primary channel

For most contractors, Data-Driven Attribution is the best choice if you have sufficient conversion volume. It accounts for the full customer journey, including searches that happen days or weeks before the final conversion.

Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) Dashboard

Build a weekly dashboard that tracks these metrics:

  • Impression Share: The percentage of eligible impressions you received. Target 60%+ for core keywords.
  • Click-Through Rate (CTR): Clicks divided by impressions. Home services average 6.37%.
  • Cost Per Click (CPC): Total spend divided by clicks. Varies by trade and market.
  • Conversion Rate: Conversions divided by clicks. Target 5%+ on desktop, 3%+ on mobile.
  • Cost Per Lead (CPL): Total spend divided by conversions. Benchmark against your trade average.
  • Lead-to-Appointment Rate: Appointments booked divided by leads. Target 40-60%.
  • Cost Per Booked Job: Total spend divided by booked jobs. This is your north star metric.
  • Return on Ad Spend (ROAS): Revenue divided by ad spend. Target 4:1 or higher.

Weekly and Monthly Review Cycles

Weekly (30 minutes): Review search terms report and add negative keywords. Check CPL by campaign and ad group. Pause any keyword with 50+ clicks and zero conversions. Review call recordings for lead quality.

Monthly (2 hours): Analyze conversion rates by device, location, and time of day. Adjust bids and budgets based on performance. Test new ad copy variations. Review landing page heatmaps and session recordings. Update seasonal messaging.

Quarterly (4 hours): Conduct a full account audit. Review keyword performance and restructure underperforming campaigns. Test new landing pages. Adjust annual budget allocations based on seasonal trends. Benchmark against industry data.

Common PPC Mistakes That Cost Contractors Thousands Every Month

After auditing hundreds of contractor Google Ads accounts, we see the same mistakes repeatedly. These are not edge cases. They are the norm. Fixing any one of them can save you thousands of dollars per month. Fixing all of them transforms your PPC from a cost center into a profit engine.

Mistake 1: Sending All Traffic to the Homepage

This is the most expensive mistake in contractor PPC. Your homepage is designed for everyone: returning customers, job seekers, partners, and prospects. It has navigation menus, multiple CTAs, and general information. A PPC landing page is designed for one person with one specific need. Service-specific landing pages convert at 6-12%. Homepages convert at 1-3%. If you are spending $5,000 per month and sending traffic to your homepage, you are losing 50-75% of your potential leads.

Fix: Build dedicated landing pages for each service line. Match the headline to the ad. Remove navigation. Include one clear CTA. Add trust signals. Test and iterate.

Mistake 2: Ignoring Negative Keywords

Most contractor accounts have fewer than 50 negative keywords. A properly built account has 300 or more. Without negative keywords, you pay for searches like "plumber jobs," "how to fix a leaky faucet," "HVAC training certification," and "free roof repair for seniors." Industry data shows that weak negative keyword management wastes 30-50% of budget.

Fix: Build your negative keyword list before launching. Use the three-layer architecture: universal negatives, search-specific exclusions, and trade-specific negatives. Review the search terms report weekly. Every irrelevant query becomes a new negative keyword.

Mistake 3: Running Ads Without Call Tracking

If 60-70% of your leads come from phone calls and you are not tracking them, you have no idea which keywords, ads, or campaigns are working. You are optimizing based on incomplete data. We have seen contractors pause high-performing campaigns because they only tracked form submissions and assumed the campaign was failing.

Fix: Implement call tracking on day one. Use Dynamic Number Insertion. Set minimum call duration for conversions. Record calls for quality review. Integrate with your CRM.

Mistake 4: Using Broad Match Without Control

Broad match keywords are Google's default, and they are dangerous for contractors. Without aggressive negative keywords, broad match triggers ads for "plumber salary," "electrician training," "roofing DIY," and "HVAC jobs near me." We have audited accounts where 40% of broad match clicks were completely irrelevant.

Fix: Start with phrase match and exact match only. Use broad match only after you have 50+ monthly conversions, a robust negative keyword list, and Smart Bidding enabled.

Mistake 5: Starting on Smart Bidding Too Early

Smart Bidding strategies like Target CPA and Maximize Conversions require data to work. Google's algorithms need 30-50 conversions per month to optimize effectively. Starting with Target CPA on day one is like asking a GPS to navigate without a map. It will make guesses, and they will be expensive.

Fix: Launch with Manual CPC or Enhanced CPC. Run for 30-45 days to gather conversion data. Switch to Smart Bidding only after you have consistent conversion volume and a stable cost per lead.

Mistake 6: Targeting Outside Your Service Area

Google's default location setting is "People in or regularly in your targeted locations." This sounds right, but it includes people who work in your area but live 50 miles away. For a contractor who only serves a 20-mile radius, this burns budget on unqualified clicks.

Fix: Change location targeting to "People in or regularly in your targeted locations" and add radius targeting around your actual service area. Exclude cities and zip codes you do not serve. Review geographic performance monthly and adjust bids.

Mistake 7: Weak or Generic Ad Copy

"Quality Service Since 1998" is not a headline. It does not match search intent. It does not create urgency. It does not differentiate you from the ten other contractors on the page. Generic ad copy kills CTR, which lowers Quality Score, which raises CPC.

Fix: Write headlines that match the exact search query. Include service, location, urgency, and offer. Test multiple angles. Refresh copy every 6-8 weeks.

Mistake 8: Optimizing on Tiny Sample Sizes

"This keyword got 10 clicks and no conversions. Pause it." No. Ten clicks is not data. It is noise. Making decisions on fewer than 30 clicks per keyword leads to killing winners and keeping losers.

Fix: Wait for statistical significance before making decisions. For keywords, aim for 50-100 clicks or 5-10 conversions before judging performance. Use confidence interval calculators if you are unsure.

Mistake 9: Treating PPC as a Set-It-and-Forget-It Channel

PPC is not a billboard. It is a live auction where your competitors change bids, Google updates algorithms, and consumer behavior shifts seasonally. An account that is not actively managed degrades by 15-25% per quarter.

Fix: Schedule weekly optimization time. Review search terms, add negatives, check CPL, and test new ads. Conduct monthly deep dives. Hire an agency if you cannot commit the time.

Mistake 10: Not Connecting PPC to Sales Outcomes

Cost per lead is a vanity metric if those leads never book. We have seen contractors celebrate a $40 CPL while their sales team converts only 5% of those leads. Meanwhile, a competitor with a $120 CPL closes 40% and generates 3x more revenue.

Fix: Track cost per booked job, not just cost per lead. Integrate PPC with your CRM. Calculate ROAS. Optimize for revenue, not clicks.

Advanced PPC Tactics for Contractors Ready to Scale

Once your foundational campaigns are profitable, these advanced tactics can help you capture more market share, lower your cost per acquisition, and build a sustainable competitive advantage.

Remarketing: Stay Top-of-Mind During Long Decision Cycles

Home services with high ticket prices and longer sales cycles, like kitchen remodels, full HVAC replacements, and roofing projects, benefit enormously from remarketing. A homeowner who visits your "Kitchen Remodeling" page but does not convert is not a lost lead. They are a warm prospect who needs nurturing.

Set up remarketing lists in Google Ads for visitors to specific service pages. Show them display ads and YouTube ads with messaging like "Still Planning Your Kitchen Remodel? Get Your Free Design Consultation" or "See Our Latest Kitchen Transformations." Remarketing CTR on Google Display averages 0.65%, but RLSA (Remarketing Lists for Search Ads) averages 5.2% with 15-22% lower CPCs.

For contractors, the optimal remarketing strategy is:

  • Display remarketing: 5-7 impressions per week to past visitors. Rotate creatives every 10-14 days.
  • RLSA: Bid on competitor brand names and broader service terms for past visitors only.
  • YouTube remarketing: Show 15-30 second before/after project videos to past site visitors.

Allocate 10-20% of your total PPC budget to remarketing. It typically delivers the lowest cost per acquisition of any campaign type.

Performance Max with Search Themes

Performance Max (PMax) is Google's automated campaign type that runs across Search, Display, YouTube, Gmail, Maps, and Discover. In 2026, PMax accounts for 45% of all Google Ads conversions. For contractors, PMax works best as a supplement to Search campaigns, not a replacement.

The key to making PMax work for contractors is using Search Themes. In 2026, Google allows up to 25 Search Themes per asset group. Use them to guide PMax toward contractor-relevant searches. Examples: "emergency plumbing repair," "kitchen remodeling contractor," "HVAC installation near me," "roof replacement financing."

Also use audience signals. Upload your CRM customer list to train PMax on what your best customers look like. In 2026, Google removed the minimum list size requirement for Customer Match, making this accessible to smaller contractors.

PMax requires a minimum budget of approximately $1,500-$2,500 per month to generate enough data for optimization. Below that threshold, stick with Search campaigns.

Hyper-Local Targeting and Radius Bidding

Not all neighborhoods convert equally. Use radius bidding to focus spend on your highest-converting areas. If your data shows that leads within 5 miles of your office book at 3x the rate of leads 15 miles away, increase bids by 25% for the close radius and decrease by 20% for the far radius.

Go deeper than city-level targeting. Target zip codes and even specific neighborhoods. A roofing contractor in Dallas should bid differently for Highland Park (high home values, frequent hail damage) versus South Dallas (different housing stock, different needs).

Weather and Event-Based Campaign Triggers

Home services are event-driven. HVAC breaks during heat waves. Roofs leak after hail storms. Pipes burst in freezes. Smart contractors adjust PPC spend in real-time based on local conditions.

When the National Weather Service issues a heat advisory, increase HVAC repair bids by 30-50%. When hail is reported in your service area, launch emergency roofing campaigns within hours. When temperatures drop below freezing, surge plumbing emergency spend. Contractors who use weather triggers see 15-25% better engagement and 20-30% lower cost per lead during peak demand windows.

First-Party Data and Offline Conversion Import

With third-party cookies deprecated, first-party data is your most valuable asset. Collect email addresses and phone numbers with clear value exchange: "Get your instant estimate" or "Download our HVAC maintenance checklist."

Then use offline conversion import to push CRM data back into Google Ads. When a lead from "emergency plumber Phoenix" converts into a $1,200 job, import that revenue into Google Ads. The algorithm learns to find more customers like that one. Businesses using offline conversion import report 15-25% improvement in cost per acquisition.

Competitor Conquesting (With Caution)

Bidding on competitor brand names can capture high-intent traffic, but it is expensive and risky. Competitor brand keywords typically have low Quality Scores (2-4) because your ad is not relevant to their brand. This means high CPCs and low ad positions.

Use competitor conquesting selectively. Target only your top 2-3 competitors. Write ads that highlight your differentiators, not attack the competitor. Send traffic to a dedicated comparison landing page. Set a separate budget cap so competitor bidding does not drain your core campaign funds. Monitor cost per lead closely and pause if it exceeds 2x your average.

Getting Started: Your First 30 Days of Contractor PPC

If you are starting from zero, here is the exact 30-day roadmap to launch profitable PPC for contractors.

Week 1: Foundation

  • Set up Google Ads account and billing
  • Install Google Tag Manager on your website
  • Set up conversion tracking for form submissions and phone calls
  • Implement call tracking with Dynamic Number Insertion
  • Connect Google Ads to Google Analytics 4
  • Build your initial keyword list using Google Keyword Planner
  • Create your three-layer negative keyword list

Week 2: Build

  • Create dedicated landing pages for your top 2-3 services
  • Write Responsive Search Ads with 12+ headlines and 4 descriptions per ad group
  • Set up all relevant ad extensions: call, location, sitelinks, callouts, structured snippets
  • Build campaign structure: one campaign per service line, tightly themed ad groups
  • Set location targeting to your actual service area with radius limits
  • Configure bidding: Manual CPC with max CPC caps

Week 3: Launch

  • Launch campaigns with daily budgets that generate at least 15-20 clicks per day
  • Verify impressions and clicks are flowing
  • Check that call tracking numbers are displaying correctly
  • Confirm conversion tracking is recording form submissions and calls
  • Begin adding obvious negative keywords from early search term data

Week 4: Optimize

  • Review search terms report: target less than 5% irrelevant traffic
  • Isolate early winners: move converting search terms to exact match
  • Pause keywords with 50+ clicks and zero conversions
  • Review call recordings for lead quality
  • Check CPL by campaign and ad group
  • Adjust bids based on early performance data

Month 2-3: Scale

  • Once you have 30+ conversions per month, test Target CPA bidding
  • Add new ad variations and test angles
  • Expand to additional service lines
  • Launch Local Services Ads if your trade qualifies
  • Integrate CRM for closed-loop attribution

Month 4+: Dominate

  • Add Performance Max as a supplement to Search campaigns
  • Launch remarketing for high-ticket services
  • Implement geographic bid adjustments based on conversion data
  • Test seasonal budget surges
  • Conduct quarterly full account audits

Frequently Asked Questions About PPC for Contractors

How much should a contractor spend on Google Ads?

Most contractors need at least $1,500-$3,000 per month in ad spend to generate consistent data and leads. Growth-focused contractors typically spend $3,000-$5,000 per month. Established multi-location companies often spend $5,000-$10,000 or more. The minimum depends on your trade and market: emergency plumbing in Los Angeles requires more budget than handyman services in a rural area. Start with what you can afford, focus on one or two service lines, and scale as you prove ROI.

How long does it take to see results from PPC?

Leads can start within 24-48 hours of campaign launch. However, campaign optimization takes 60-90 days. Google's algorithms need 30-50 conversions to learn what works. During the first month, expect higher costs per lead as the system gathers data. By month three, a well-managed account should be hitting stable benchmarks. Do not judge performance after one week.

What is a good cost per lead for contractors?

It varies dramatically by trade. Pools and spas average $45 per lead. Roofing averages $228. The number that actually matters is cost per booked job. A $228 roofing lead that closes a $15,000 job is far more valuable than a $47 cleaning lead for a $150 service. Calculate your target CPL by dividing your average job value by your close rate and your target ROAS. If your average job is $5,000, you close 25% of leads, and you want 4:1 ROAS, your max CPL is $500.

Should I do PPC myself or hire an agency?

If your monthly ad spend is under $1,500 and you have time to learn, DIY is feasible. Above $2,000 per month, a specialized agency usually pays for itself through lower CPL and higher lead quality. The average contractor wastes 30-50% of their budget on common mistakes that an experienced agency avoids. Look for agencies with contractor-specific case studies, transparent reporting, and no long-term contracts.

What is the difference between Google Ads and Local Services Ads?

Google Ads (Search) is a pay-per-click model. You write ads, choose keywords, and pay when someone clicks. Local Services Ads (LSAs) is a pay-per-lead model. Google verifies your license and insurance, displays a Google Verified badge, and charges you only when a customer calls or messages. LSAs appear above Search Ads and typically have lower cost per lead but less control over messaging. The best strategy is running both together.

Why are my clicks so expensive?

High CPCs usually come from one of four problems: bidding on broad match keywords without negative keywords, low Quality Score from weak ad relevance or poor landing pages, competing for generic terms instead of specific services, or operating in a highly competitive market. Fix your match types, improve your Quality Score, target long-tail keywords, and use geographic bid adjustments to reduce CPCs by 20-40%.

How do I track if PPC is actually working?

Track four levels of metrics: traffic (clicks, CTR), leads (forms, calls, CPL), sales (appointments booked, cost per booked job), and revenue (ROAS, revenue per lead). The most important metric is cost per booked job. Implement call tracking, form tracking, and CRM integration to connect every click to revenue. Without this, you are optimizing based on incomplete data.

What are negative keywords and why do they matter?

Negative keywords prevent your ads from showing for irrelevant searches. Without them, you pay for clicks from job seekers, DIYers, students, and people looking for free services. A comprehensive negative keyword list can reduce wasted spend by 30-50%. Build your list before launching and expand it weekly based on search term reports.

Can PPC work for small contractors with limited budgets?

Yes, but focus is critical. With $1,500 per month, target one service line in a tight geographic area. Use exact match keywords for your highest-intent terms. Build one excellent landing page. Track every call and form. Do not spread your budget across ten services and five cities. Concentrated spend beats diluted spend every time.

What is Quality Score and how do I improve it?

Quality Score is a 1-10 rating that measures the relevance of your keywords, ads, and landing pages. It directly impacts your cost per click and ad position. Improve it by writing ads that match your keywords exactly, building dedicated landing pages for each service, and ensuring fast mobile load times. Each point increase reduces CPC by approximately 8-10%.

Should I bid on my own brand name?

Yes, especially if competitors are bidding on it. Branded search campaigns typically have Quality Scores of 8-10 and CPCs under $2. They protect your brand real estate and capture high-intent traffic. Even if you rank #1 organically, having a paid ad at the top increases total CTR and prevents competitors from stealing your customers.

How often should I update my ad copy?

Refresh ad copy every 6-8 weeks to combat creative fatigue. CTR typically drops 15-20% after 8 weeks as the same audience sees the same ads. Keep your top-performing headlines and replace the bottom 30%. Update seasonal messaging quarterly: "Beat the Heat" in summer, "Winter-Ready Furnace Check" in fall.

What is the best bidding strategy for contractors?

Start with Manual CPC or Enhanced CPC for the first 30-45 days. This gives you control while gathering conversion data. Once you have 30+ conversions per month, switch to Target CPA. Set your target based on actual cost-per-booked-job data, not guesswork. With 100+ conversions and revenue tracking, consider Target ROAS.

How do I compete with big companies like HomeAdvisor and Angi?

You do not compete on brand awareness. You compete on specificity and trust. Big directories run generic ads. You run ads for exact services in exact neighborhoods. You use your real company name, real reviews, and real local phone number. You send traffic to dedicated landing pages, not category pages. Homeowners often prefer hiring a local contractor directly over going through a lead generation middleman. Your job is to make that choice obvious.

Your 30-Day Action Plan to Profitable Contractor PPC

PPC for contractors is not a mystery. It is a system. When you understand how the auction works, target the right keywords, write ads that match search intent, build landing pages that convert, track every lead to revenue, and optimize relentlessly, you build a predictable lead generation engine that works while you sleep.

Here is what to do in the next 30 days:

  • This week: Audit your current PPC account or set up a new one. Install call tracking and conversion tracking. Build your negative keyword list.
  • Next week: Create dedicated landing pages for your top 2-3 services. Write Responsive Search Ads with message match. Set up all relevant ad extensions.
  • Week 3: Launch campaigns with focused budgets. Monitor search terms daily. Add negatives aggressively.
  • Week 4: Review performance. Calculate your actual cost per lead and cost per booked job. Adjust bids, pause losers, and scale winners.

The contractors who win at PPC are not the ones with the biggest budgets. They are the ones who treat it as a system, measure what matters, and optimize continuously. The framework in this guide has been tested across hundreds of contractor accounts. It works when you work it.
